opus-5.5.text:
I think the key difference is where the intelligence for using the tool actually lives.

In the LangChain era, around 2023, the model itself didn't really know how to use tools. What people did was build a scaffold around it: you wrote a workflow, a chain, maybe a ReAct-style prompt template, and you told the model, "first call this search API, then parse the result, then decide among these three branches." The planning was largely done by the human engineer who designed the pipeline. The model was more like a component that filled in slots. It could follow the format, but if something unexpected happened, say the search returned garbage, or the task needed five steps instead of three, the whole thing tended to break. So those agents were brittle, and they didn't really get better as you gave them more compute or more steps.

With reasoning models, the situation changed in a fundamental way. Through reinforcement learning, the model learns to think in a long chain of thought, and tool calls become part of that thinking process itself. The model decides on its own when to search, when to run code, how to read the result, whether the result is trustworthy, and whether it should backtrack and try a different approach. Tool use is no longer an external procedure attached to the model; it's an action inside the model's own reasoning loop. And importantly, it's trained end to end with outcome rewards, so the model actually learns from the consequences of its tool calls, rather than just imitating a format.

So I'd summarize it this way: the old agents were human-designed workflows with a model inside, and the new agents are models that have internalized the workflow. One consequence is scaling. With the reasoning-era approach, giving the model more turns, more tokens, more interaction with the environment actually makes it stronger, because it learned to use that budget. That's something the LangChain-style systems never really had.

r001.rationale: It describes LangChain-era agents as human-designed workflows, chains, and pipelines around the model.

r002.rationale: It says tool calls become part of the model’s thinking and reasoning loop.

r003.rationale: It says reinforcement learning trains the model to decide when to call tools and that outcome rewards teach it from the consequences of those calls.

fable-5.1.text:
The distinction, to me, comes down to where the decision-making lives.

When people built agents with LangChain, the intelligence of the system was mostly in the scaffolding. You, the engineer, wrote the chain. You decided: first call the search tool, then parse the result, then call the calculator, then summarize. The model was essentially a very good text-filling component inside a workflow that a human had already designed. If the task deviated from what you anticipated, the whole thing broke, because the model had no real say in the control flow. It was tool use by script, with the LLM as a subroutine.

Reasoning-era agents flip that. The model itself holds the plan. It thinks before it acts, it decides which tool to call and why, it looks at the result and decides whether that result is good enough or whether it needs to try something else. The loop of observe, think, act, re-evaluate is happening inside the model's own reasoning, not in your Python code. So the scaffold becomes very thin. You give it a set of tools and a goal, and it figures out the sequence.

The practical consequence is huge. In the LangChain era, adding a new capability meant redesigning the chain. Now, adding a capability mostly means exposing a new tool and describing it well. The model generalizes to new combinations you never wrote down.

There's a second difference that I think people underrate: error recovery. A scripted agent has no notion that it failed unless you wrote an explicit check. A reasoning agent notices that the search returned nothing useful, or that the code threw an exception, and it adjusts. That ability to recover from its own mistakes is what makes long-horizon tasks possible at all. Without it, errors compound and anything beyond five or six steps falls apart.

And this comes from training, not from prompt engineering. The models were trained with reinforcement learning on multi-step tasks where tool calls were part of the trajectory, so the tool use is baked into how they reason rather than bolted on from outside.

So the short version: before, humans did the reasoning and the model did the talking. Now the model does the reasoning, and the humans mostly just build the tools.

r001.rationale: It describes LangChain-era agents as human-written chains with predetermined tool-call sequences.

r002.rationale: It says the reasoning-era model decides which tool to call and treats tool use as part of its own reasoning loop.

r003.rationale: It says reinforcement learning trains models on multi-step tasks involving tool calls, but does not say the model chooses to call a tool based on whether doing so improves its reinforcement-learning objective.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is who controls the workflow. In many of the agents people built with LangChain, the developer had already defined much of the process: retrieve some information, call a tool, pass the result into another prompt. The model could make choices, but those choices often sat inside a fairly prescribed workflow.

With reasoning-era agents, you can give the model a goal and let it decide more of the intermediate steps. It can choose a tool, examine the result, realize its initial approach was wrong, and try something else. Tool use becomes part of an ongoing reasoning process, rather than just a step in a chain.

That’s not a strict distinction between LangChain and reasoning models—you can build that kind of agent using LangChain, too. The change is in how much planning and adaptation the model can reliably handle. And that shifts the engineering work toward giving it good tools, useful feedback, and clear boundaries.

r001.rationale: It describes LangChain agents as having developer-defined processes such as retrieving information, calling a tool, and passing the result to another prompt.

r002.rationale: It says reasoning-era agents can choose tools and treat tool use as part of an ongoing reasoning process.

r003.rationale: It does not mention reinforcement learning or choosing tool calls based on whether they improve an RL objective.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is who decides the workflow. In many early LangChain applications, the developer specified most of it: retrieve some documents, call the model, invoke a tool, then pass the result to the next step. The model was one component inside a program whose structure we had already designed.

With reasoning-era agents, we give the model a goal and a set of tools, and it can decide what to do next based on what it discovers. It might call a tool, examine the result, realize an assumption was wrong, and change its approach. Tool use becomes part of an iterative problem-solving process.

But this isn’t a strict LangChain-versus-reasoning distinction. You can build that kind of agent with LangChain, and earlier agents also had tool-selection loops. What has changed is how reliably the model can carry out those loops—planning, interpreting feedback, and recovering from mistakes. That lets developers delegate more of the workflow, while still putting limits and checks around it.

r001.rationale: It describes early LangChain applications as developer-specified sequences of retrieval, model calls, and tool invocations.

r002.rationale: It says reasoning-era models receive tools and can choose to call them as part of an iterative problem-solving process.

r003.rationale: It does not mention reinforcement learning or choosing tool calls based on whether they improve an RL objective.
